triage.name: Coronary Artery Disease
triage.reason: Core cardiology diagnosis reachable from chest pain history, risk factors, exam, ECG and troponin; drives major management decisions.

presentation: older format without SNOMED terms
exam: older format without SNOMED terms

demographics: Men tend to develop symptomatic CAD about a decade earlier than women
Women often present around or after menopause, and microvascular disease is more common in women
Prevalence rises steadily with age in both sexes
Higher rates among non-Hispanic White and non-Hispanic Black adults than among some other US groups

risk_factors.text: Current or past smoking or tobacco use
Family history of early heart disease in a parent or sibling
Chronic inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis or lupus

comorbidities: Prior stroke or transient ischemic attack
family_history: Heart attack, bypass surgery, or stent in a parent or sibling before age 50–55
Sudden cardiac death in a close relative
social_history: Sedentary work and little leisure exercise
High chronic stress or long work hours

chief_complaints.text: I get this pressure in my chest when I walk up the stairs
My chest feels tight and heavy when I exert myself
I get short of breath doing things I used to do easily
I feel a squeezing in the middle of my chest that goes into my left arm
I just feel worn out and can't keep up anymore

hpi.onset: Gradual over weeks to months; often first noticed during a specific activity
hpi.duration: Symptoms usually present for weeks to months when stable; minutes to hours when unstable
hpi.progression: Stable pattern: predictable discomfort with a similar level of exertion, relieved within minutes by rest. Unstable pattern: symptoms come on with less effort, last longer, or occur at rest — a change from the usual pattern
hpi.location: Mid-chest or substernal, sometimes described as the whole chest or upper abdomen
hpi.radiation: May spread to the left shoulder and arm, both arms, neck, jaw, back, or upper abdomen
hpi.quality: Pressure, tightness, squeezing, heaviness, or a band-like sensation; often not described as sharp pain
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate, typically 3–6/10; severe and unrelenting when it represents an acute coronary syndrome
hpi.timing: Comes on with exertion, emotional stress, cold weather, or after a heavy meal; lasts 2–10 minutes with stable angina and resolves with rest or nitroglycerin

associated_symptoms.text: Shortness of breath with the chest discomfort
Sweating or clamminess during an episode
Nausea or a queasy stomach during an episode

pertinent_negatives: Chest pain that is sharp and stabbing
Pain that changes with breathing, coughing, or twisting the torso
Pain reproduced by pressing on the chest wall
Pain that is worst when lying flat and better sitting forward
Burning pain that follows meals and wakes them at night
Pain that comes only with swallowing
Sudden tearing pain that started at maximum intensity
Pain that is only in one small spot and lasts seconds

negatives: Chest pain at rest in the stable pattern
Pain reproduced by pressing on the chest
argues_against: Sharp positional pain worsened by breathing
Pleuritic chest pain with a recent viral illness
Sudden shortness of breath with leg swelling and recent immobility
Burning pain that wakes them at night and improves with antacids
Pain that comes only with swallowing
Focal neurologic deficits suggesting a cerebrovascular cause

negatives: Pain worse with arm movement or twisting
argues_against: Reproducible chest wall pain on palpation
Pain that follows a fall or strain

general.mild: Comfortable, no distress at rest; normal habitus or overweight
general.moderate: Mildly uncomfortable when describing exertional symptoms, otherwise comfortable at rest
general.severe: Diaphoretic and anxious, clutching the chest, prefers to sit upright
general.critical: Ill-appearing, pale and clammy, agitated or lethargic, may be hypotensive

findings.maneuver: Palpate the anterior chest wall and reproduce symptoms by pressing on the sternum and ribs
findings.finding: No reproducible chest wall tenderness

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the four valve areas with the diaphragm and bell
findings.finding: Normal S1 and S2 without murmur, rub, or gallop

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the apex with the bell in the left lateral decubitus position
findings.finding: Fourth heart sound (atrial gallop)

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the apex with the bell
findings.finding: Third heart sound suggesting left ventricular dysfunction

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the apex with the diaphragm
findings.finding: Holosystolic murmur radiating to the axilla

findings.maneuver: Auscultate over the carotid arteries and palpate the upstroke
findings.finding: Carotid bruit or diminished upstroke, suggesting concomitant atherosclerosis

findings.maneuver: Inspect the internal jugular vein at 45 degrees
findings.finding: Elevated jugular venous pressure suggesting heart failure
Bibasilar crackles suggesting pulmonary congestion
Clear breath sounds without crackles or wheeze

findings.maneuver: Press over the dorsum of each foot and the pretibial area
findings.finding: Pitting edema suggesting right heart failure

findings.maneuver: Palpate the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses
findings.finding: Diminished or absent pedal pulses suggesting peripheral artery disease

findings.maneuver: Inspect the eyelids, elbows, knees, and Achilles tendons
findings.finding: Xanthelasma or tendon xanthomas suggesting familial hypercholesterolemia

findings.maneuver: Measure temperature and inspect for systemic signs
findings.finding: Afebrile without rash or joint swelling

labs.caveat: Normal or unchanged serial troponin supports stable angina rather than an acute coronary syndrome; a rise or fall indicates myocardial injury. Interpret against the 99th percentile for sex.
A key modifiable risk factor and target for statin therapy; very high values suggest familial hypercholesterolemia.
Screens for diabetes, a major risk factor and driver of outcomes.
Baseline kidney function guides medication dosing and contrast use before angiography.
Anemia worsens myocardial oxygen supply and demand and can precipitate angina.
Elevated when CAD has led to heart failure; helps distinguish cardiac from pulmonary causes of dyspnea.
Thyroid disease can mimic or aggravate angina; check when the picture is atypical.

findings.finding: Normal sinus rhythm
Horizontal or downsloping ST depression during symptoms or with exercise
T wave inversion in the affected territory
ST elevation with a territorial pattern indicating acute transmural injury
Pathologic Q waves from prior infarction
Tall peaked hyperacute T waves early in transmural injury
Left bundle branch block or other intraventricular conduction delay
Left ventricular hypertrophy from chronic hypertension
Atrial fibrillation
Prolonged QT interval

imaging.study: Coronary angiography (invasive, with or without CT angiography)

findings.text: Focal or diffuse luminal narrowing of one or more epicardial coronary arteries
Obstructive disease defined as 50% or greater stenosis of a major artery
Nonobstructive disease with less than 50% stenosis
Multivessel or left main disease
Calcified or mixed plaque on CT angiography
No significant epicardial stenosis despite symptoms (suggests microvascular disease)
Regional wall motion abnormality in a coronary distribution
Normal resting wall motion (does not exclude CAD)
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Reduced left ventricular ejection fraction
Left atrial enlargement or diastolic dysfunction
Mitral regurgitation

imaging.study: Exercise or pharmacologic stress testing with imaging (nuclear perfusion or stress echocardiography)

findings.text: Reversible perfusion defect in a coronary territory during stress
Stress-induced regional wall motion abnormality
Fixed defect suggesting prior infarction
Normal study

imaging.preferred_when: Lower-risk patients with atypical symptoms and no known CAD

findings.text: Coronary artery calcification and stenosis
High negative predictive value when no plaque is seen
Coronary calcium score quantifying plaque burden
Usually normal heart size and clear lungs
Cardiomegaly or pulmonary venous congestion when heart failure is present

initial.why: First test in any chest pain; identifies ischemia, injury, or prior infarction
Distinguishes acute coronary syndrome from stable angina; serial measurements if elevated or symptoms ongoing
Anemia can worsen ischemia; baseline before procedures
Kidney function, electrolytes, and glucose before medications or contrast
Establishes LDL target and need for statin therapy
Screens for diabetes, a major risk factor
Assesses wall motion, ejection fraction, and alternative causes of chest pain

confirmatory.test: Exercise or pharmacologic stress testing with imaging (nuclear perfusion or stress echocardiography)
confirmatory.why: Confirms inducible ischemia in stable patients who can exercise or need pharmacologic stress
confirmatory.only_if: stable symptoms and no high-risk features

confirmatory.test: Coronary angiography (invasive, with or without CT angiography)
confirmatory.why: Definitive anatomic diagnosis and allows revascularization
confirmatory.only_if: high-risk features, refractory symptoms, or positive stress test
lower-risk patient with atypical symptoms and no known CAD

supporting.why: Supports heart failure as a complication when dyspnea is prominent
Thyroid disease can mimic or aggravate angina
Evaluates alternative causes of chest pain and heart size
supporting.only_if: dyspnea, fever, or concern for a noncardiac cause

supporting.why: Rules out pulmonary embolism when the presentation is ambiguous
supporting.only_if: pleuritic pain, hypoxemia, or Wells score suggests PE

not_indicated.why: Not needed unless pain is epigastric or suggests pancreatitis
No role in the evaluation of chest pain from CAD

decision_points: Any patient with ongoing chest pain and ST elevation or dynamic changes goes to emergency reperfusion without waiting for further testing
A single normal troponin does not exclude acute coronary syndrome; repeat serially
Stress testing is avoided in unstable patients; proceed to angiography
Check kidney function before contrast angiography
Consider microvascular disease when symptoms are typical but angiography shows nonobstructive disease

criteria.name: Obstructive CAD
criteria.summary: A major epicardial coronary artery narrowed by 50% or more on angiography, reducing blood flow and causing exertional ischemia.
items: 50% or greater stenosis of a major coronary artery
Symptoms or objective evidence of ischemia

criteria.name: Nonobstructive CAD
criteria.summary: Atherosclerotic plaque narrowing a major artery by less than 50%, which can still cause symptoms or progress.

criteria.name: Coronary microvascular disease
criteria.summary: Ischemia from dysfunction of the small coronary vessels despite normal or near-normal epicardial arteries; more common in women.
items: Typical angina or ischemia on testing

differential.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
differential.why_considered: Burning substernal discomfort that can radiate to the chest and is sometimes triggered by meals or exertion

history: Burning or sour taste, worse after meals and when lying flat
Relief with antacids or acid suppression
No consistent relationship to exertion
No radiation to the arm or jaw
exam: Epigastric tenderness without chest wall tenderness
ecg: Normal sinus rhythm without ischemic ST-T changes

differential.name: Pulmonary embolism
differential.why_considered: Acute chest discomfort with shortness of breath and tachycardia can mimic myocardial ischemia
differential.trigger: Pleuritic pain, hypoxemia, or sudden dyspnea with a risk factor such as recent immobility, surgery, or active cancer

history: Sudden onset of dyspnea
Pleuritic pain worse with deep breaths
Recent immobility, surgery, or prior venous thromboembolism
Hemoptysis
exam: Tachycardia out of proportion to the chest findings
Unilateral leg swelling or calf tenderness
labs: Elevated D-dimer when pretest probability is low or intermediate
Troponin may be mildly elevated from right heart strain
imaging: Filling defect in the pulmonary arteries on CT angiography
ecg: S1Q3T3 pattern or right axis deviation
T wave inversion in the right precordial leads

differential.name: Aortic dissection
differential.why_considered: Severe chest pain that can radiate to the back or abdomen and be mistaken for cardiac ischemia
differential.trigger: Sudden tearing pain that reaches maximum intensity at onset, or a pulse or blood pressure difference between arms

history: Abrupt onset reaching peak intensity within seconds
Tearing or ripping quality
Pain migrating to the back or abdomen
History of hypertension or connective tissue disease
exam: Blood pressure or pulse difference between arms
New diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation
Focal neurologic deficit or pulse deficit
labs: Troponin usually normal or only mildly elevated
imaging: Intimal flap on CT angiography, MRI, or transesophageal echocardiography
ecg: ST elevation only if the dissection involves a coronary ostium

differential.name: Pericarditis
differential.why_considered: Chest pain in a similar location that can be mistaken for angina, especially in younger patients

history: Sharp pain worse with deep breaths, coughing, or lying flat
Better when sitting up and leaning forward
Recent viral illness
Pleuritic quality
labs: Troponin may be mildly elevated from myopericarditis
ecg: Diffuse PR depression and widespread concave ST elevation

differential.name: Costochondritis
differential.why_considered: Anterior chest pain that patients may describe as pressure and that is common in younger adults

history: Pain is sharp and localized to a small area
Worse with twisting, reaching, or pressing on the chest
No relationship to exertion or relief with rest
exam: Reproducible tenderness over the costochondral junctions

differential.name: Esophageal spasm
differential.why_considered: Severe substernal pressure that can be indistinguishable from angina and may occur at rest

history: Pain unrelated to exertion
May occur with swallowing, hot or cold liquids
Coexists with reflux symptoms
labs: No ischemic changes on stress testing
imaging: Esophageal manometry shows spasm if pursued
ecg: Normal or nonspecific changes without a territorial pattern

differential.name: Anxiety or panic attack
differential.why_considered: Chest tightness, palpitations, and shortness of breath that can resemble cardiac ischemia, especially in younger patients

history: Episodes peak within minutes and resolve spontaneously
Associated with fear, paresthesias, or a sense of doom
Occurs at rest or during stress rather than with a fixed exertion threshold
exam: Tachypnea, tremulousness, no cardiac murmur or gallop
ecg: Sinus tachycardia without ischemic ST-T changes

differential.name: Anemia
differential.why_considered: Fatigue, exertional dyspnea, and chest discomfort from reduced oxygen delivery can mimic angina

history: Progressive fatigue and pallor
Heavy menstrual bleeding, dark stools, or known blood loss
Symptoms improve with correction of anemia

severity.mild: Stable angina with predictable symptoms only at high levels of exertion; normal resting ECG and troponin; preserved ejection fraction
severity.moderate: Stable angina at moderate exertion with risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes, or dyslipidemia; may have ST depression or T wave changes on ECG and mild left ventricular hypertrophy
severity.severe: Unstable angina or non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction with symptoms at rest or with minimal exertion; dynamic ST changes and rising troponin; possible heart failure signs
severity.critical: ST-elevation myocardial infarction or cardiogenic shock with ongoing ischemic pain, hypotension, pulmonary edema, or malignant arrhythmia requiring emergency reperfusion

red_flags.finding: Chest pain at rest or lasting more than 20 minutes
red_flags.meaning: Acute coronary syndrome; needs immediate ECG and troponin and possible emergency reperfusion

red_flags.finding: ST elevation on ECG in a territorial pattern
red_flags.meaning: Acute transmural myocardial infarction; activate the catheterization laboratory

red_flags.finding: Hypotension with cool extremities and pulmonary congestion
red_flags.meaning: Cardiogenic shock; urgent revascularization and hemodynamic support

red_flags.finding: New murmur of mitral regurgitation with pulmonary edema
red_flags.meaning: Papillary muscle rupture or severe ischemic mitral regurgitation; surgical emergency
Life-threatening arrhythmia from acute ischemia; defibrillate and treat ischemia

red_flags.finding: Sudden tearing pain with pulse or blood pressure difference between arms
red_flags.meaning: Aortic dissection, not CAD; avoid antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy until excluded

complications.name: Acute myocardial infarction
clues: Pain at rest lasting more than 20 minutes

complications.name: Heart failure
clues: Bibasilar crackles and elevated jugular venous pressure

complications.name: Arrhythmia including atrial fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia
Sudden cardiac death
clues: Prior myocardial infarction with reduced ejection fraction

complications.name: Ischemic mitral regurgitation
clues: New holosystolic murmur at the apex

complications.name: Ventricular aneurysm
clues: Abnormal cardiac silhouette on chest x-ray

special_populations.differences: Symptoms are often atypical, such as dyspnea, fatigue, confusion, or falls rather than classic chest pain; higher risk of silent infarction and worse outcomes.
Autonomic neuropathy blunts anginal warning symptoms, so ischemia may present silently or as dyspnea; higher rates of multivessel disease and worse prognosis.

Chest pain is usually noncardiac, but pregnancy increases thrombotic risk; spontaneous coronary artery dissection is an important cause of peripartum myocardial infarction and requires a different management approach.
Higher prevalence of CAD and calcified vessels; contrast exposure during angiography requires hydration planning and careful medication dosing.
More likely to have diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidemia; exercise stress testing may be limited by deconditioning, so pharmacologic stress imaging is often preferred.

key_questions.question: What does the discomfort feel like, and where is it?
key_questions.looking_for: Substernal pressure, tightness, squeezing, or heaviness rather than sharp or stabbing pain

key_questions.question: Does it spread anywhere?
key_questions.looking_for: Radiation to the left shoulder and arm, both arms, neck, jaw, back, or upper abdomen

key_questions.question: What brings it on?
key_questions.looking_for: Exertion, emotional stress, cold weather, heavy meals, or sexual activity

key_questions.question: What makes it go away, and how long does it last?
key_questions.looking_for: Relief within minutes with rest or nitroglycerin; episodes lasting 2 to 10 minutes in stable angina

key_questions.question: Has the pattern changed recently — does it now come with less effort, last longer, or happen at rest?
key_questions.looking_for: A change from a stable pattern suggests unstable angina or acute coronary syndrome and needs urgent evaluation

key_questions.question: How long have you had this, and is it getting worse over time?
key_questions.looking_for: Weeks to months of gradually worsening exertional symptoms in stable disease

key_questions.question: Do you get short of breath, sweat, feel nauseated, or feel lightheaded during an episode?
key_questions.looking_for: Associated dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, or lightheadedness supporting cardiac ischemia

key_questions.question: Do you have high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, or kidney disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Major modifiable risk factors that raise the likelihood of CAD

key_questions.question: Have you ever smoked or used tobacco?
key_questions.looking_for: Current or past smoking, a strong risk factor

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had a heart attack, bypass surgery, or a stent, especially before age 50 to 55?
key_questions.looking_for: Early heart disease in a parent or sibling, or familial hypercholesterolemia

key_questions.question: What medications do you take, including over-the-counter pain relievers and any hormones?
key_questions.looking_for: NSAIDs, estrogen, testosterone, or prednisone that can raise cardiovascular risk; also antianginal and lipid-lowering therapy already in use

key_questions.question: Does the pain change with breathing, coughing, twisting, or pressing on your chest?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent in typical angina; present suggests a musculoskeletal or pleural cause

key_questions.question: Does the pain happen only with meals, when lying flat, or with swallowing?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent in typical angina; present suggests reflux or esophageal spasm

key_questions.question: Have you had chest pain that does not go away, or that happens while you are resting?
key_questions.looking_for: Rest pain or pain lasting more than 20 minutes suggests acute coronary syndrome and requires emergency evaluation

reasoning_points: Exertional substernal pressure that radiates to the arm, neck, or jaw and resolves with rest or nitroglycerin
Presence of major risk factors such as hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, smoking, older age, and family history of early heart disease
No reproducible chest wall tenderness and no positional or pleuritic component
ECG showing ischemic ST depression or T wave inversion, or a prior infarction pattern
Troponin normal or unchanged in stable disease, or rising in acute coronary syndrome
Atherosclerotic plaque with 50% or greater stenosis of a major coronary artery on angiography, or nonobstructive plaque with evidence of ischemia
Alternative life-threatening causes such as pulmonary embolism and aortic dissection considered and excluded
Risk factors and symptom pattern used to estimate pretest probability and guide stress testing versus anatomic imaging

easy: Older man with classic exertional substernal pressure radiating to the left arm
Relief with rest and nitroglycerin within minutes
Multiple risk factors such as hypertension, smoking, and high cholesterol
Ischemic ST depression on ECG during symptoms
medium: Woman around menopause with exertional dyspnea and fatigue rather than chest pain
Older adult with exertional symptoms but a normal resting ECG
Patient with diabetes and atypical or silent ischemia
Symptoms overlap with reflux, requiring careful characterization of the exertional pattern
hard: Typical angina with nonobstructive coronary arteries suggesting microvascular disease
Younger patient with a strong family history and familial hypercholesterolemia
Patient with chronic kidney disease and calcified vessels limiting CT angiography interpretation
Presentation with heart failure or arrhythmia as the first sign of CAD
Chest pain in a patient with a competing diagnosis such as pulmonary embolism or aortic dissection
